definition: Grandmaster Chess is a computer chess game published for MS-DOS in 1992.
details: It was developed by IntraCorp and its subsidiary Capstone Software that was focused on neural network technology and an artificial intelligence able to learn from mistakes. The original release of the game includes VGA and SVGA support, multiple skill levels, different sets of pieces, boards and backgrounds, 2D/3D view, pull-down menus, ability to rewind and replay moves, and a rating of the player's strength. A 1993 CD-ROM version adds Terminator 2: Judgment Day: Chess Wars, an animated chess set like Battle Chess, as a tie-in with the film Terminator 2: Judgment Day. In 2021, a Windows port of the original was released as Grandmaster Championship Chess.

explainer.lead: Grandmaster Chess is a 1992 MS-DOS chess game built around an AI opponent that was intended to learn from its mistakes using neural network technology. It also packaged chess in an unusually flexible presentation, with multiple difficulty levels, board styles, and 2D or 3D views.

tiers.eli5: Grandmaster Chess is like a chess partner living inside a computer, with settings that let you choose how challenging the game should be. You can change how the board looks, watch from different angles, and go back over moves. Its makers also designed its computer opponent to learn from mistakes.
tiers.practitioner: The game exposes practical controls such as multiple skill levels, VGA or SVGA graphics, 2D and 3D views, move rewind and replay, and a player-strength rating. Its AI is described as using neural network technology and learning from mistakes, but no architecture, training procedure, or measurable playing strength is specified.
tiers.paperLevel: Grandmaster Chess can be described as a computer-chess system whose opponent selects moves within a standard chess game and was designed to improve by learning from mistakes using neural network technology. The available description does not establish a network architecture, objective function, learning algorithm, or evaluation results.

explainer.example: A beginner could select a lower skill level and a 2D board, play a game against the computer, then rewind a losing sequence and replay the moves to examine where the position changed. The game could also provide a rating of that player's strength.

explainer.intuition: The central idea is to make a chess program feel like an adaptable opponent rather than only a fixed move calculator. Around that opponent, the game provides ways to adjust the challenge, inspect earlier moves, and estimate the player's strength.
howItWorks: The player chooses settings such as skill level, pieces, board, background, and viewing mode.
The player and computer opponent take turns making chess moves.
The opponent uses AI described as neural-network-based and able to learn from mistakes.
Moves can be rewound and replayed, and the game provides a rating of the player's strength.
explainer.whyItMatters: It is an example of an early-1990s commercial game presenting neural-network-based, mistake-learning AI as part of its chess opponent. Its later CD-ROM edition and Windows port also show how the original game was repackaged and preserved.
misconceptions: The title refers to a computer game, not to a person holding the chess title of grandmaster.
The description does not establish that its neural network used the techniques or scale of modern chess engines.
Chess Wars was an animated addition to the 1993 CD-ROM edition, not the original 1992 release.
